buckets.title: Vector direction and unit representation
buckets.badge_reason: The arithmetic is short, but learners commonly lose quadrant information, treat i/j notation as new physics, or try to normalize the zero vector.

conventions.statement: Declare +x/+y before interpreting component signs or reporting a direction.
Normalize only a nonzero vector; the zero vector has no unit direction.

scope.covers: Translate 2-D signed components into i-hat/j-hat notation, recover direction from component signs plus an acute inverse-trigonometric reference angle, and normalize a nonzero 2-D vector to unit direction.
excluded: General dot product and scalar projection.

capabilities.action: Use an inverse tangent on a positive right-triangle ratio to recover an acute reference angle, leaving quadrant selection to the consuming subject.
capabilities.success_criterion: Given positive leg magnitudes a and b, evaluate or represent alpha = tan^-1(b/a) as an acute reference angle and state that this reference angle still requires the consuming subject to place it in the directed geometry. Draft bridge only; Mathematics-provider acceptance remains required.

capabilities.action: Translate a 2-D signed component pair into i-hat/j-hat notation and back without changing the vector.
capabilities.success_criterion: Given declared x/y axes, write (v_x,v_y) as v_x i-hat + v_y j-hat with signs preserved, and recover the same component pair from that notation.

capabilities.action: Recover the direction of a nonzero 2-D vector from its signed x/y components using quadrant information plus an acute inverse-trigonometric reference angle.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify the quadrant or axis from component signs, obtain an acute reference angle from |v_y/v_x| when both components are nonzero, and place that angle in the correct directed quadrant rather than reporting tan^-1(v_y/v_x) blindly.

capabilities.action: Normalize a nonzero 2-D vector to a dimensionless unit vector in the same direction.
capabilities.success_criterion: Compute or retain the vector magnitude |v|>0, divide every signed component by that same magnitude, express the result consistently, verify magnitude 1, and refuse normalization when v is the zero vector.

microtopics.title: Translate signed components to i-hat/j-hat notation
microtopics.badge_reason: The notation is compact but can tempt learners to drop a negative coefficient or treat basis labels as extra vector magnitudes.
entry_assumptions: Can read signed x/y components against declared positive axes.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The component pair and v_x i-hat + v_y j-hat are two notations for the same 2-D vector; coefficients carry the same signs and units as the original components.

teaching_path.action: Declare +x and +y and identify i-hat with the +x unit direction and j-hat with the +y unit direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: The basis symbols are meaningless without the axes they name.
teaching_path.output: i-hat = +x unit direction; j-hat = +y unit direction

teaching_path.action: Replace the ordered pair (v_x,v_y) by v_x i-hat + v_y j-hat, carrying each coefficient sign unchanged.
teaching_path.why_valid: The coefficients are exactly the signed components along the two basis directions.

teaching_path.action: Read the two coefficients back from the i-hat/j-hat expression and compare with the original component pair.
teaching_path.why_valid: A notation translation is correct only if the original signed components are recovered.
teaching_path.output: recovered pair equals the starting pair

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A negative coefficient should be made positive because i-hat and j-hat already contain the direction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If v_x is negative while +x is declared to the right, what sign must multiply i-hat?
misconceptions.repair: Keep the coefficient sign. The hat symbol names the positive basis direction; a negative coefficient reverses that component.

exit_task.prompt: With declared +x/+y axes, a vector has components (a,-b), where a and b are positive. Write it in i-hat/j-hat notation and state how you would recover the component pair.

answer.summary: v = a i-hat - b j-hat, and the coefficients recover the pair (a,-b).
reasoning: i-hat names +x and j-hat names +y.
The x component is +a, so its coefficient is +a.
The y component is -b, so its coefficient is -b.
answer.check: Read the two signed coefficients back; they must be exactly (a,-b).

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer is a symbolic representation translation and asserts no computed numerical value.

microtopics.research_contribution: Owner-approved ExamSIDE Vector Algebra demand makes compact unit-basis notation a useful preparation action. The teaching is locally authored and does not import dot/cross-product content.

predict.prompt: If the y-component is negative, should the coefficient of j-hat be positive or negative?
predict.defensible_answer: Negative; j-hat names +y, so a negative coefficient is required for a component pointing against +y.

attempt.produces: A one-line translation from a signed component pair to i-hat/j-hat notation.
attempt.model_response: Preserve each component as the coefficient of its matching basis vector, including its sign.

task.prompt: With +x to the right and +y upward, express each of the following in i-hat/j-hat notation and recover the component pair: (A) (4, −7), (B) (0, −3), (C) (−6, −2).

route.why_this_ask: It anchors the notation to the declared axis.

route.ask: What signed number multiplies that basis symbol?
route.why_this_ask: It forces the learner to carry the original component sign into the new notation.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The learner route begins from the coefficient decision and reconstructs the notation from axis meaning rather than being shown the completed expression first.

boundary_test.prompt: If the x-component is zero, what happens to the i-hat term?
boundary_test.answer: Its coefficient is zero, so the term may be written as 0 i-hat or omitted without changing the vector.
boundary_test.confirms: The notation represents components rather than requiring both basis terms to appear visibly.

independent_checks.statement: Read the two coefficients back from the i-hat/j-hat form; they must match the original signed component pair exactly.
Test a case where the x-component is zero; the i-hat term has zero coefficient and may be omitted without changing the vector.

compact_anchor.prompt: A vector has components (−2, 5). Write it in i-hat/j-hat notation.
compact_anchor.result: v = −2 i-hat + 5 j-hat. The negative coefficient carries the direction information; i-hat and j-hat are unit basis vectors, not extra positive multipliers.

microtopics.title: Recover direction from signed components
microtopics.badge_reason: The ratio is simple, but a calculator's inverse tangent does not by itself preserve quadrant information.
entry_assumptions: Can use an inverse tangent to obtain an acute reference angle through the declared Mathematics bridge.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Direction recovery is two-stage: component signs locate the quadrant or axis, while inverse tangent of the positive component-magnitude ratio supplies only an acute reference angle to place inside that quadrant.

teaching_path.action: Use the signs of v_x and v_y to identify the quadrant or an exact axis before taking any ratio.
teaching_path.why_valid: The signs retain directional information that a ratio can lose.
teaching_path.output: quadrant or axis fixed from signs

teaching_path.action: When both components are nonzero, form the positive ratio |v_y|/|v_x| and obtain the acute reference angle alpha = tan^-1(|v_y|/|v_x|).
teaching_path.why_valid: The absolute component magnitudes form the legs of the right triangle; inverse tangent returns the acute reference angle, not the full directed angle.

teaching_path.action: Place alpha in the previously identified quadrant and report the requested directed angle or verbal direction.
teaching_path.why_valid: Quadrant placement restores the signs discarded by the positive ratio.
teaching_path.output: quadrant I: theta=alpha; quadrant II: theta=180°-alpha; quadrant III: theta=180°+alpha; quadrant IV: theta=360°-alpha for standard 0°<=theta<360° reporting

teaching_path.action: Check that the reported direction has the same x/y sign pattern as the original components.
teaching_path.why_valid: Any correct direction must point into the same quadrant or axis as the signed component pair.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The value tan^-1(v_y/v_x) is always the final direction angle.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If v_x<0 and v_y>0, can a negative raw ratio by itself tell you that the vector lies in quadrant II?
misconceptions.repair: Fix the quadrant from the component signs first. Use an acute reference angle from absolute component magnitudes, then place it in that quadrant.

exit_task.prompt: A nonzero vector has v_x<0, v_y>0 and |v_y|<|v_x|. State its quadrant, write the acute reference-angle expression, and show how the directed angle from +x is obtained symbolically.

answer.summary: It lies in quadrant II. Let alpha = tan^-1(|v_y|/|v_x|); the standard directed angle from +x is 180 degrees - alpha.
reasoning: Negative x and positive y place the vector in quadrant II.
The positive magnitude ratio gives only the acute reference angle alpha.
Quadrant II places that reference angle above the -x direction, giving 180 degrees - alpha from +x.
answer.check: The final angle must have cosine negative and sine positive, matching the original component signs.
acceptable_alternatives: State the direction as alpha above the -x axis instead of using a 0-360 degree angle.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer is symbolic and asserts no computed numerical angle.

microtopics.research_contribution: ExamSIDE Vector Algebra demand exposes direction/resultant-orientation questions that are not closed by magnitude or component decomposition alone. The route keeps inverse-trig readiness explicit as a Mathematics bridge.

predict.prompt: A vector has negative x-component and positive y-component. Before using a calculator, which quadrant must the answer lie in?

attempt.produces: A quadrant decision, an acute reference-angle expression, and a directed-angle placement.
attempt.model_response: Use signs first for quadrant, then alpha = tan^-1(|v_y|/|v_x|), then place alpha in that quadrant.

task.prompt: A vector has components v_x = −5 and v_y = −12. (a) Identify its quadrant from the component signs alone, before any trigonometry. (b) Write the positive-magnitude ratio and the acute reference-angle expression. (c) State the standard directed angle from +x (0°–360° convention). Justify each step.

route.ask: What do the two component signs tell you before any trigonometry?
route.why_this_ask: It preserves the directional information a ratio can erase.

route.ask: Which positive leg ratio gives the acute angle to the x-axis?
route.why_this_ask: It separates reference-angle recovery from quadrant placement.

route.ask: How must that acute angle be placed in the quadrant you already fixed?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents the calculator output from becoming the direction by default.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The learner commits to a quadrant before seeing the inverse-trig construction, so the calculator cannot become the source of direction.

boundary_test.answer: The vector points exactly along +y; report that axis direction directly and do not divide by v_x.
boundary_test.confirms: Axis cases are handled directly rather than forced through an invalid ratio.

independent_checks.statement: Verify that the reported direction has the same x/y sign pattern as the original component pair.
Check an axis-aligned case (one component = 0): report the exact axis direction without dividing by zero.

compact_anchor.prompt: A vector has v_x = −4 and v_y = 3. State its quadrant and the expression for its acute reference angle.
compact_anchor.result: Quadrant II (negative x, positive y). Acute reference angle: alpha = arctan(3/4). Directed angle from +x = 180° − alpha.

microtopics.title: Normalize a nonzero vector to unit direction
microtopics.badge_reason: The division is simple, but the same magnitude must divide every component and the zero vector is a hard domain boundary.
entry_assumptions: Can express the vector in signed components or i-hat/j-hat notation.
Can obtain the nonnegative magnitude from perpendicular components through the declared Mathematics bridge.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Dividing every component of the same nonzero vector by its positive magnitude removes units and scale while preserving the component ratio and therefore the direction.

teaching_path.action: Confirm that the vector is nonzero and identify its positive magnitude |v|.
teaching_path.why_valid: Normalization divides by |v|, so |v| must be greater than zero.

teaching_path.action: Divide every signed component by the same magnitude: v_hat = (v_x/|v|) i-hat + (v_y/|v|) j-hat.
teaching_path.why_valid: Multiplication by the same positive scalar reciprocal changes length but preserves direction and component signs.

teaching_path.action: Recompute the magnitude of the normalized components and confirm it is 1.
teaching_path.why_valid: A unit vector is defined to have magnitude 1.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A unit vector keeps the original physical unit because it points in the same direction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If every component is divided by a magnitude carrying the same unit, what unit remains in the ratio?
misconceptions.repair: The units cancel. A unit vector carries direction and has magnitude 1; it is dimensionless in this representation.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The zero vector can be normalized by dividing each zero component by its magnitude.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: What is the magnitude of the zero vector, and what denominator would normalization require?
misconceptions.repair: Its magnitude is zero, so normalization would divide by zero. The zero vector has no unit direction.

exit_task.prompt: A nonzero vector has symbolic components (a,b) and magnitude M>0. Write its unit-direction vector in component and i-hat/j-hat form, then give the magnitude check.

answer.summary: The unit direction is (a/M,b/M) = (a/M)i-hat + (b/M)j-hat, and its magnitude is 1.
reasoning: M is the positive magnitude of the original nonzero vector.
Dividing both components by the same positive M preserves direction.
answer.check: Confirm M>0 first; if M=0 the normalization is undefined.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer is symbolic; the magnitude-one check is algebraic and asserts no computed numerical measurement.

microtopics.research_contribution: The owner-approved Vector Algebra demand supports unit-direction preparation, but this microtopic keeps the operation bounded to 2-D normalization and explicitly rejects the zero-vector case.

predict.prompt: If every component of a nonzero vector is divided by its own magnitude, does its direction change?
predict.defensible_answer: No. A positive common scale factor changes length but not direction.

attempt.produces: A normalized symbolic vector plus a magnitude-one check.
attempt.model_response: Use v_hat=v/|v| only when |v|>0, divide every signed component by the same |v|, and verify the new magnitude is 1.

task.prompt: A displacement vector has components d_x = −9 m and d_y = 12 m. (a) State whether this vector can be normalized and why. (b) Compute |d|. (c) Write the unit-direction vector in component and i-hat/j-hat form. (d) Verify the result has magnitude 1.
givens: State the non-zero condition explicitly before dividing.

route.ask: What denominator must be shared by both components if only the scale is to change?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents component-wise rescaling that would rotate the vector.

route.ask: What must be true of that denominator before division?
route.why_this_ask: It exposes the zero-vector domain boundary.

route.ask: What magnitude should the result have?
route.why_this_ask: It gives the independent closure criterion.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The learner starts from the invariance requirement—same direction, new length 1—and reconstructs the shared scaling factor rather than receiving the formula first.

boundary_test.prompt: Can the zero vector be normalized?
boundary_test.answer: No. Its magnitude is zero, so v/|v| would divide by zero and the zero vector has no direction to preserve.
boundary_test.confirms: The normalization relation is domain-restricted to nonzero vectors.

independent_checks.statement: Recompute the magnitude of the normalized vector: sqrt((v_x/|v|)² + (v_y/|v|)²) must equal 1.
Confirm |v| > 0 before dividing; explicitly reject normalization for the zero vector.

compact_anchor.prompt: A vector has components (6, 8). Compute its unit-direction vector.
compact_anchor.result: |v| = 10. v-hat = (6/10) i-hat + (8/10) j-hat = 0.6 i-hat + 0.8 j-hat. Magnitude check: sqrt(0.36 + 0.64) = 1.

relations.meaning: A two-dimensional vector expressed on declared perpendicular x/y axes can be written equivalently as the signed x coefficient times the +x unit basis vector plus the signed y coefficient times the +y unit basis vector.

symbols.meaning: Dimensionless unit basis vector along declared +x
Dimensionless unit basis vector along declared +y

conditions: The x and y axes are declared and perpendicular.
i_hat and j_hat name the positive unit directions of those axes.
The signed coefficients retain the physical units of the vector components.

derivation.action: Treat i-hat and j-hat as the +x and +y unit basis directions.
derivation.why_valid: A basis direction identifies where each component acts.

derivation.action: Attach the signed x/y components as coefficients of their matching basis vectors.
derivation.why_valid: The coefficients are precisely the vector's components on those axes.

limits: This notation does not define a dot product or cross product.
It does not by itself determine a direction angle.
checks: Reading the coefficients back must recover the original signed component pair.

relations.expression: alpha = arctan(|v_y|/|v_x|); component signs determine the quadrant
relations.meaning: For a nonzero vector with both perpendicular components nonzero, inverse tangent of the positive component-magnitude ratio gives an acute reference angle; the signed components independently determine the quadrant in which that reference angle must be placed.

symbols.meaning: Acute reference angle to the x-axis

conditions: When both components are nonzero, use positive component magnitudes for the acute ratio.
If either component is zero, report the exact axis direction directly rather than dividing by zero.
Quadrant selection comes from component signs, not from the inverse-tangent output alone.

derivation.action: Use component signs to identify the quadrant or axis.
derivation.why_valid: The signs are the directional information carried by the component pair.

derivation.action: For nonzero v_x and v_y, use tan(alpha)=|v_y|/|v_x| and invert the tangent.
derivation.why_valid: The absolute components form the legs of the right triangle for the acute reference angle.

derivation.action: Check that the placed direction has the original x/y sign pattern.
derivation.why_valid: A direction in the wrong quadrant cannot reproduce the signed components.

limits: The formula shown supplies an acute reference angle, not a quadrant-complete calculator shortcut.
The zero vector has no direction angle.
This relation does not introduce dot products, projections or cross products.
checks: Direction quadrant agrees with signs of v_x and v_y.
Axis cases are handled without a zero denominator.

relations.meaning: Dividing a nonzero vector and every signed component by the same positive magnitude produces a dimensionless vector of magnitude 1 in the same direction.

symbols.meaning: Unit vector in the direction of v

conditions: Every component is divided by the same magnitude.
The component axes and basis notation refer to the same declared frame.

derivation.why_valid: The zero vector has zero magnitude and no direction to normalize.

derivation.action: Multiply the vector by the positive scalar 1/|v|.
derivation.why_valid: A positive scalar changes length but preserves direction.

derivation.action: Apply the magnitude relation to the normalized components.
derivation.why_valid: The resulting magnitude must equal 1 by definition of normalization.

limits: This normalization does not create a new physical dimension or unit.
It does not require a direction angle to be computed first.
checks: The signs and component ratio match the original vector.

questions.stem: With +x declared to the right and +y declared upward, a vector has components v_x = 3 and v_y = −4. Write the vector in i-hat/j-hat notation. Then recover the component pair from that notation.

reasoning: i-hat names +x; j-hat names +y.
v_x = 3 → coefficient of i-hat is +3.
v_y = −4 → coefficient of j-hat is −4.
Written: v = 3 i-hat − 4 j-hat.
Recovery: coefficients of i-hat and j-hat are 3 and −4 respectively — matching the original pair.
answer.check: Read the two signed coefficients back; they must be exactly (3, −4).

questions.failure_signal: If your answer wrote a positive coefficient for j-hat despite v_y = −4, check the sign: j-hat names +y, so a component pointing against +y needs a negative coefficient.

family_exposure.closure: You preserved a negative component sign when translating to i-hat/j-hat notation and recovered the original pair by reading coefficients.

difficulty.basis: Notation translation with a negative y-component; requires preserving the negative coefficient of j-hat.

questions.stem: A vector has components v_x = −3 and v_y = 4 with +x to the right and +y upward. (a) State the quadrant the vector lies in from the component signs alone. (b) Write the acute reference-angle expression using positive component magnitudes. (c) State the directed angle from +x (standard 0°–360° convention).
conditions: +x: right, +y: up. Standard angle from +x, measured counter-clockwise.

reasoning: (a) v_x < 0, v_y > 0 → quadrant II.
(b) Both components nonzero → use positive magnitudes: alpha = arctan(|4|/|3|) = arctan(4/3).
(c) Quadrant II: directed angle from +x = 180° − alpha ≈ 180° − 53.1° ≈ 126.9°.
answer.check: Direction in quadrant II must have negative cosine and positive sine — matching v_x < 0 and v_y > 0.
acceptable_alternatives: State "alpha above the −x axis" instead of 180° − alpha.

questions.failure_signal: If your directed angle is in quadrant I or III, recheck the component signs: v_x < 0 and v_y > 0 place the vector strictly in quadrant II.

family_exposure.closure: You fixed the quadrant from component signs, formed the acute reference angle, and placed it correctly in quadrant II.

difficulty.basis: Two-stage direction recovery: quadrant from signs then acute reference angle placed in quadrant II.

questions.stem: A vector has components v_x = 3 and v_y = 4. (a) Compute its magnitude. (b) Write the unit-direction vector in component and i-hat/j-hat form. (c) Verify that the result has magnitude 1.
conditions: State the condition on |v| before dividing.

reasoning: (b) Divide every component by 5: v-hat = (3/5) i-hat + (4/5) j-hat.
(c) Magnitude check: sqrt((3/5)² + (4/5)²) = sqrt(9/25 + 16/25) = sqrt(25/25) = 1.
answer.check: |v| > 0 confirmed before dividing. Unit vector magnitude = 1 verified.
acceptable_alternatives: (0.6) i-hat + (0.8) j-hat is acceptable as a decimal form.

questions.failure_signal: If your unit vector has components (3, 4) without division, you did not divide by the magnitude. Divide every signed component by 5.

family_exposure.closure: You confirmed |v| > 0, divided both components by the same magnitude, and verified the resulting vector has magnitude 1.

difficulty.basis: 3-4-5 normalization; requires magnitude-first, divide-both-components, verify-unit-magnitude sequence.

questions.stem: A velocity vector is written as v = −5 i-hat + 0 j-hat m/s with +x to the right. (a) State the signed x- and y-components. (b) Describe the direction of the velocity in words. (c) Can this vector be normalized? If so, write the unit-direction vector.

answer.summary: (a) v_x = −5 m/s, v_y = 0. (b) Exactly along −x (to the left). (c) |v| = 5 > 0; unit direction = −1 i-hat + 0 j-hat = −i-hat.
reasoning: (a) Coefficients: −5 for i-hat, 0 for j-hat → v_x = −5 m/s, v_y = 0.
(b) v_y = 0 means no y-component; v_x < 0 means exactly along −x. Direction: to the left.
(c) |v| = sqrt((−5)² + 0²) = 5 ≠ 0; v-hat = (−5/5) i-hat + (0/5) j-hat = −i-hat + 0 j-hat = −i-hat.

hints.text: The y-component is 0: the vector lies exactly on an axis. What axis, and in which direction?
Magnitude = sqrt(v_x² + v_y²). Then divide both components by the same magnitude.

questions.failure_signal: If your unit-direction answer was +i-hat instead of −i-hat, check the sign: the x-component is −5, so dividing by magnitude 5 gives −1, not +1.

family_exposure.closure: You read components from notation, identified an axis-aligned vector, and computed a unit direction for a pure-axis vector with a negative non-zero component.

difficulty.basis: Axis-aligned vector with a zero component and a negative non-zero component; normalization gives −i-hat as a result that is easy to sign-flip incorrectly.

questions.stem: A velocity vector is given as v = −3 i-hat − 3 j-hat m/s with +x to the right and +y upward. (a) State the quadrant and identify any symmetry between the component magnitudes. (b) Write the unit-direction vector for v. (c) Determine the acute reference angle and hence the directed angle from +x (0°–360° convention). (d) State whether the unit-direction vector you found and the directed angle describe the same direction. Justify.
conditions: +x: right, +y: up. v_x = −3 m/s, v_y = −3 m/s.

answer.summary: (a) QIV→ actually QIII; (b) −(1/√2) i-hat − (1/√2) j-hat; (c) alpha = 45°, directed = 225°; (d) yes.
reasoning: (a) v_x < 0 and v_y < 0 → quadrant III. Both components have the same magnitude, so the vector lies at 45° from both axes.
(c) alpha = arctan(|−3|/|−3|) = arctan(1) = 45°. Quadrant III: directed angle = 180° + 45° = 225°.

(d) A direction of 225° from +x has cosine negative and sine negative (matching v_x < 0, v_y < 0). The unit vector −(1/√2)(i-hat + j-hat) also points into quadrant III. Both describe the same direction.
answer.check: Check the magnitude of v-hat: sqrt((1/√2)² + (1/√2)²) = sqrt(1/2 + 1/2) = 1. Correct.
acceptable_alternatives: Exact form −(√2/2) i-hat − (√2/2) j-hat is equivalent.
State direction as "45° below the −x axis" instead of 225°.
subpart_answers: (a) Quadrant III; both component magnitudes equal 3 (symmetric about the −x = −y line).
(d) Yes; both characterizations point into quadrant III with equal-magnitude negative components.

rubric.criterion: Quadrant identified from signs before any trigonometry.
Normalization uses the same magnitude for both components.
Reference angle placed in quadrant III correctly.

hints.text: Both components are negative: identify the quadrant from signs before any calculation.
Because |v_x| = |v_y|, the reference angle is arctan(1) = 45°. Which quadrant offset applies?

questions.failure_signal: If your directed angle is 45° (quadrant I result), you applied the reference angle without the quadrant offset. Both components are negative, placing the vector in quadrant III; the standard 0°–360° angle is 180° + 45° = 225°.

family_exposure.closure: You combined direction recovery, normalization, and representation reconciliation for a quadrant-III symmetric vector.

transfer.statement: Both components are negative (quadrant III, not II) and equal in magnitude, so the reference angle is the familiar 45°. The learner must simultaneously normalize and recover direction, then reconcile both representations.
transfer.invariant: Signs are checked before trigonometry; the reference angle is always acute; the same magnitude divides all components.

novelty.why_new: Q-VDU-1A-DIRECTION-01 (Core1A anchor) recovers direction for quadrant II. Q-VDU-1A-UNIT-01 normalizes a quadrant-I vector. No prior item requires simultaneously normalizing AND recovering direction for the same vector, nor does any prior item use quadrant III. The equal-magnitude components (45° reference angle) are a distinct structural case not present in earlier items. The reconciliation demand in part (d) is genuinely new: no Core1A or Core2A item asks the learner to confirm that unit-direction and directed-angle representations are consistent.

difficulty.basis: Quadrant III with equal-magnitude components; requires normalization + direction recovery + representation reconciliation.
